title: Not a better wrestler
hookLine: someone may out-wrestle you, but not be kinder or more modest (Meditations 7.52)

cards: There's always someone better. Better at your job, better at tennis, better at small talk; better-looking, better paid. Your cousin got the promotion.
Your old classmate wrote the book. The comparison machine never runs out of fuel, because there's always another name to feed it. Marcus Aurelius didn't try to smash the machine.
In book seven he used a picture from the wrestling ground to switch it to a different contest entirely.

teach.b: In Meditations seven, fifty-two, Marcus admits it plainly: someone else may be better at throwing an opponent. Some people really are more talented than you at things.
But, he says, that person is not more devoted to the common good.
Not more modest. Not better trained to meet whatever happens. Not more considerate of other people's faults.
Four contests, and none of them depends on your body, your luck or your talent.
Marcus doesn't kill the urge to compete; he moves it. If you're going to outdo people, outdo them in the things entirely in your power. You can't choose to be taller or quicker.
You can choose to be more patient with a coworker's mistakes.

teach.h: A CONTEST WHERE OTHERS WIN TOO.
teach.b: In that contest anyone can win, and nobody has to lose. There's a trick hiding inside it: when you compete in kindness, the other person benefits from your winning.
Paul's letter to the Romans has a neighboring line, in the King James words: "in honour preferring one another." Different tradition, with its own reasons and its own meaning.
So when the comparison machine starts up, let it. Then ask it a different question. Not who's better.

how: Readers of Marcus sometimes redirect envy into a contest of character, asking who can be most patient or considerate in a situation rather than who is most talented.

o: a straw floor where Roman soldiers slept on the march
the wrestling ground, where someone may throw better than you
a rug spread out for guests at a Roman dinner

games.q: not a better wrestler — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus claims to be the best wrestler in Rome
he admits someone else may be better at throwing an opponent.
Marcus lists being considerate of others' faults as a contest worth winning
alongside being social, modest and ready for whatever happens.

games.q: your cousin got the promotion you wanted, and the envy stings. what's Marcus's move?
o: work out how to beat them next time.
compete instead in patience, modesty and kindness.
games.why: Meditations 7.52: someone may throw an opponent better, but not be more modest or more considerate. Compete there.

practice: Bring to mind someone you tend to compare yourself to, and let the comparison come, with its sting. Then change the contest: could I be more patient than them today, more modest, more forgiving of others' mistakes?
Pick one, and picture it in one real moment.

wordCard.voice: Mat. Someone else may beat you there, Marcus admits, but no one can stop you being kinder or more modest. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: out-kind them. In that contest, nobody has to lose. That's day five hundred ninety-three.
